newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Rescued yachtsman tells wife he will return to sea.
newsitem.headline: Rescued yachtsman tells wife he will return to sea.

text.p: Rescued solo yachtsmen Tony Bullimore told his wife on Monday he had his next sailing project in mind when they were reunited in Perth after his dramatic rescue from the freezing Southern Ocean.
"No, it's nice and easy," he joked when his wife, Lalel, smilingly complained about his plans during their meeting at British Consul-General's residence in Perth.
The meeting was exclusively televised by Australia's Seven Network.
The survival story of the 56-year-old former Royal Marine was attracting big commercial interest from newspapers, television and movie studios.
Earlier on Monday, Bullimore and French sailor Thierry Dubois stepped on land to a rapturous welcome, cheered by thousands of dockside well-wishers as they gave thanks for their lives.

Channel Seven later showed Bullimore and Lalel hugging and kissing as he told his wife: "Careful, don't stand on my feet", referring to frostbite from his four days under the upturned hull of his yacht.
Asked by a Channel Seven reporter if he would sail in another solo, round-the-world race, he said, nodding at Lalel: "Well, if I can get permission. I don't think there's any doubt about it."
Lalel said she had never given up hope. "I knew the old bulldog would come home," she said.
A crowd of several thousand turned out on a sunny morning to greet the two solo sailors who capsized in rough seas during the Vendee Globe round-the-world race eight days ago.

The crowd waved British and Australian flags, sang Waltzing Matilda, and held up banners saying "Welcome Home Heroes" as the Australian navy frigate Adelaide made its way into the western port of Fremantle.
"Thank you Australia for giving me back my life," Bullimore said after walking gingerly down the gangplank of the Adelaide.
"I'm slightly emotional about this, but I'm going to turn around and say this 'thank you guys'," he said, raising his arms and pointing to the ship's crew at a quayside reception.
Frenchman Dubois also paid tribute to the ship and aircraft crews involved in the rescue of the round-the-world yachtsmen from freezing Antarctic seas last Thursday.
But he denied the two were heroes.
"I don't like a lot the word hero. We are not heroes. I think Australia have a lot of heroes on this ship and in the aircraft that saved us," Dubois said.
Bullimore was picked up after spending four days in a dark air pocket in his upturned yacht, battered by freezing seas.
His fate was unknown until he swam out from under his yacht and into the arms of rescuers.
Dubois, 29, was earlier plucked by helicopter from a tiny life-raft dropped by the Australian air force.
Another race participant, Frenchman Raphael Dinelli, was rescued from his sinking yacht in the frigid seas south of Australia the day after Christmas.

Dubois and Bullimore were swamped after the official reception by more than 150 local and international media before being whisked away to hospital, where doctors said the pair were in "extraordinarly good shape", despite their ordeal.
